## The end-of-build design audit (#16)

**User request, 2026-07-28:** after all `todo/` plans *and* the `scoping/` items are implemented, do a
full design review/audit of the product using **`impeccable`** and **`design-taste-frontend`**.

- **`impeccable` is the primary tool** — it is already configured for this repo (`.impeccable/live/config.json`)
  and reads `DESIGN.md` / `PRODUCT.md`, so it audits against *our* system ("The Midnight Atelier"), not a
  generic one. `/impeccable audit <surface>` per screen, then `polish`.
- **`design-taste-frontend` is a partial fit** — it is written for landing pages, portfolios and
  redesigns. Its audit-first redesign mode applies; its landing-page defaults do not. Fitcheck is a
  mobile-only PWA. Use it as a second opinion on "does this look templated", not as the system of record.
- **Judge at phone width, in the iOS Simulator** — never a resized desktop browser. A desktop-width
  screenshot has already produced false findings on this project once (see the occasion-row measurements
  in `docs/STATE.md`).
- **Sequencing caveat:** `scoping/2026-07-24-womens-wardrobe-scoping.md` adds one-piece garments
  (dresses/jumpsuits), which changes the flat-lay layout templates and the credits list. Auditing the
  visual system *before* that fork lands means auditing it twice. If the women's fork stays deferred
  ("a lot later"), run the audit on the menswear product and re-run the affected screens afterwards.
- Two known items are already parked for this pass: the **10–11px uppercase kickers** (deferred by
  decision 2026-07-24, see below) and the **off-ramp font sizes** the impeccable hook flags in
  `refine-sheet.tsx` / `stylist-view.tsx` / `item-card.tsx`.
- Existing drift is catalogued in `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` — read it first so the audit does
  not rediscover what is already written down.

## Open decisions blocking a plan

- **"Style an outfit with this"** (item detail, `Fitcheck.dc.html:654`) conflicts with Decision 5: looks
  are a daily drop, generated once per day, and tapping never calls the model. Styling around a chosen
  item is inherently on-demand. Does it spend an AI call per tap, consume the regenerate quota, or just
  filter the already-stored looks to ones containing that item? This decides whether the button is free
  or is the biggest per-user cost in the product.
- **Wear Stats gap analysis** — *"unlocks 14 new outfits"* is a simulation of what a hypothetical item
  would enable, not a query. Needs designing.
- **"See curated picks"** (`:767`) — a commerce/affiliate surface with no product decision behind it.

# Plan Review — 2026-07-27

_A read-through of every plan in `todo/` and `scoping/` against the code as it actually is on
`fix/generator-coverage`. Local-only (`docs/` is gitignored)._

**Why this file exists:** the plan files were edited in place during the review, and `docs/` is not in
git — so there is no diff to read afterwards. This records what changed, what was deliberately left
alone, and what was checked and found fine, so none of it has to be rediscovered.

---

## 1. Fixed in the plan files (2026-07-27)

Nine factual defects — things that would have failed on execution, not matters of taste. Already
applied; listed so they are not re-reported.

| Plan | Defect | Fix applied |
|---|---|---|
| `outfit-detail-wear-logging` | Imported `localDateKey`, which **does not exist**. The real export is `localDateFor(now, timeZone)` and it takes a required timezone. 5 call sites. | Corrected name; added the `profiles.location_timezone` read in both `toggleWear` and the page, so an evening wear in Berlin does not log to the next day — the bug the plan's own comment claimed to avoid. |
| `entitlements` | Same `localDateKey` error (2 sites). | Same fix. |
| `entitlements` | `generationsUsedToday` counted **outfit rows**. `saveDailyLooks` writes one row per *look* (3 per generation), so a free user was blocked after 1 generation, not 3. | Counts **distinct occasions** for the day. Takes `(userId, today)`; `assertCanGenerate` passes the local date the action already computed, rather than re-deriving it from the server clock. |
| `entitlements` | Task 2's test imported the `server-only` module and could not resolve under jsdom — the plan admitted this two steps later without fixing the import. | Pure functions (`entitlementsFor`, `checkGenerations`) moved into `tiers.ts`; `entitlements.ts` re-exports them; the test imports `../tiers`. |
| `seasons-soft-preference` | Task 4 Step 7 said *"replace everything from `isEligible` through the end of `buildCandidates`"* and pasted a **pre-fix** body — top-major nested loop, `slice(0, CAP)`, `outer[0]`, `accessories[0]`. Executing it reverts the coverage fix (tops 20→1, coats 3→1, accessories 3→1). | The pasted loop is gone, replaced by an explicit do-not-rewrite warning and a 4-step surgical edit list. Stale line refs and the stale `outer[0]` comment corrected. `coverage.test.ts` named in Global Constraints as the regression guard. |
| `item-signals-in-generator` | The "mild weather" test asserted the chunky/fine gap is `< 0.2`; the implementation in the same task yields **0.59** (at 18°, `want = 0.28` → 0.38 vs 0.97). The task could never go green. | Replaced with a relative assertion — the mild gap is narrower than the cold gap (0.59 < 0.65). The inaccurate `want`-sits-near-0.5 comment corrected too. |
| `route-url-audit` | Task 3 creates `app/outfits/[outfitId]/`, but `outfit-detail-wear-logging` (queue #4) already builds `app/outfits/[id]/`. Two slug names on one dynamic segment is a **Next.js build error**. | Task 3 marked superseded, collapsed into a `<details>` block, replaced by a verify-only step. File table and Task 5 text updated to `[id]`. |
| `route-url-audit` | Task 5 ends `git add CLAUDE.md docs/STATE.md` — both gitignored (`.gitignore:36`, `.gitignore:34`), so the commit fails on an empty index and the task blocks. | Replaced with "edit both, nothing to commit here". |
| `wear-stats` | `countCombos` summed `buildCandidates(...).length`, which stops at `CAP = 200` — so any sizeable closet returns 200 before *and* after the hypothetical piece, every `unlocks` is 0, and the gap card never renders for the users who would pay for it. | Counts the product of eligible required slots instead. **See §3 — the replacement formula is a judgment call, not a mechanical fix.** |
| `wear-stats` | `expect(gap === null \|\| gap.unlocks > 0).toBe(true)` is a tautology given the implementation only sets `best` when `unlocks > 0`. Cannot fail. | Asserts the real contract: any returned gap has a positive count and names a real candidate. |
| `regenerate-quota`, `cutout-backfill` | Dependency paths pointed at `plans/2026-07-22-*.md`; both files are now in `plans/done/`. | Repointed. |

---

## 2. Deliberately NOT changed — decided, not defects

Raised during the review and left alone: these are product decisions already made, or matters of taste.
Recorded so a future review does not re-open them as findings.

- **Wearing a look nulls `generated_on`, so it leaves today's set.** Correct fix for the FK problem, and
  intentional per the plan. The user-visible consequence — tap "Wear this today" and the stylist screen
  drops to two looks — is not written down anywhere, and nothing checks how `loadDailyLooks` /
  `reassembleLooks` behave with a partial set. Worth a deliberate answer when
  `outfit-detail-wear-logging` is picked up, not a plan edit now.
- **Profile hub's "outfits" stat counts every `outfits` row ever** (~12/day at 3 looks × 4 occasions),
  with no filter. Probably wants distinct days or favourites. Design call.
- **`updatePreferences` is read-modify-write**, while its comment claims it stops two open screens
  reverting each other. It doesn't — a SQL-side `preferences || $patch::jsonb` would. Near-impossible
  race for a single user; comment accuracy only.
- **`/generate` → `/today` sweep.** `README.md:37` settles the ordering (route-audit runs last), so the
  later plans hard-coding `/generate` are correct when they run. But route-audit has **no sweep task**
  for the four references they introduce: `settings.md` and `outfit-detail-wear-logging.md`
  (`revalidatePath("/generate")`), `fit-diary.md` (empty-state link), and `design-tokens.md`, whose nav
  test asserts the label `"Stylist"` that route-audit renames to `"Today"`. Add a sweep step when
  route-audit is picked up.
- **`regenerate-quota` has no rewrite banner in the file.** `README.md:31` and `MONETISATION.md:162`
  both mark it ⚠️ rewrite → Pro #1, but a worker opening only the plan file implements the superseded
  `profiles.plan` design.
- **`wear-stats` has no Pro gate.** `README.md:33` already flags this; the plan still has none.
- **README/plan drift:** `README.md:43-47` lists *"Style an outfit with this"* as an open decision
  blocking a plan, but `item-detail-rebuild.md:22-36` has already decided it (filter today's stored
  looks; fall back to a quota-consuming generation). One of the two should move.
- **`GAP_CANDIDATES` is menswear-only** (oxford, loafers, wool trousers). Consistent with the women's
  wardrobe being deferred (`README.md:56`) — flagged only so it is revisited with that work.

---

## 3. One substitution that needs your eye

`wear-stats` Task 2's `countCombos` was rewritten from "count what `buildCandidates` returns" to
"multiply the eligible required-slot counts". The **bug** was real and mechanical (the `CAP` makes the
old version return 0 for real closets). The **replacement** is a modelling choice:

- It counts *buildable* outfits, ignoring the cap — which is what *"unlocks 14 new outfits"* claims.
- It ignores outerwear and accessories entirely (`maxAccessories: 0` was already the plan's intent).
- It grows multiplicatively, so numbers get large fast on a real closet. `Grey wool trousers` in a
  20-top / 20-shoe closet reads as "+400 outfits", which is true and probably not what you want to
  print. A presentation cap, or counting only the *marginal* pieces, may be the better claim.

It also now depends on `eligibleByCategory`, which `seasons-soft-preference` creates — that dependency
has been added to the plan's constraints.

`README.md:48` already lists the gap analysis as an open decision. This is the specific technical reason
it needs one.

---

## 4. Checked and found fine — do not re-raise

- **`entitlements` adds `outfits_user_generated_idx (user_id, generated_on)`.** Not redundant with
  `outfits_daily_lookup`, which is `(user_id, occasion, generated_on)` — `occasion` is the second
  column, so it cannot serve the meter's predicate.
- **`wear_logs` FK surgery** in `outfit-detail-wear-logging` Task 1 is sound. `outfit_id` is nullable
  (`20260718090000_outfits.sql:28`), so `on delete set null` is valid, and the inline unnamed constraint
  auto-names to `wear_logs_outfit_id_fkey`, so the `drop constraint if exists` matches.
- **`Fitcheck.dc.html` authority.** `README.md:72-76` already corrects the old "byte-identical duplicate,
  ignore it" claim. `docs/STATE.md:114` still carries the stale version, and
  `item-data-completeness.md:1087` already schedules that fix.
- **`score.ts` being rewritten by two plans.** `item-signals-in-generator.md:224` explicitly says to keep
  the season term, and README orders seasons #1 / item-signals #12. Anticipated, not a conflict.
- **`fit-diary` date arithmetic.** Spot-checked: 1 July 2026 is a Wednesday (2 lead cells), 2028 is a
  leap year, the streak cases and the 204-day gathering-dust figure all compute correctly.
- **All docs cited by the plans exist**: `MONETISATION.md`, `design-review-2026-07-24.md`, `BUGS.md`,
  `prototype-review.md`, `Fitcheck.dc.html`.

---

## 5. A question the plans cannot answer themselves

`MONETISATION.md:25-29` says the daily drop **must never be gated**. `MONETISATION.md:37,76` puts the
drop inside the 3/day meter ("drop + regenerates + other occasions"). With four occasions each needing
its own generation, a free user who taps all four is blocked on the fourth — having only ever used the
product as intended, never once tapping Regenerate.

Not a bug in any plan; both readings are written down as policy. Worth resolving before `entitlements`
(queue #7) ships, since it is the plan that makes the choice real.

---

## 6. Scoping docs

All three are in good shape and correctly refuse to be plans. Two cross-links worth adding when they are

-- The daily drop (see CLAUDE.md "Decision 5"): looks are generated ONCE per
-- local day per occasion and then read back, not regenerated on every tap.
--
-- generated_on is the USER'S local date (lib/outfits/local-date.ts), never UTC.
-- look_index is the position within the day's set of three, so the order the
-- stylist chose survives a round trip.
alter table public.outfits
  add column if not exists generated_on date,
  add column if not exists look_index    smallint;

-- One row per (user, occasion, day, position). A regenerate deletes the day's
-- rows and re-inserts, so this also stops a double-submit writing six looks.
create unique index if not exists outfits_daily_unique
  on public.outfits (user_id, occasion, generated_on, look_index)
  where generated_on is not null;

-- The read path: "today's set for this occasion".
create index if not exists outfits_daily_lookup
  on public.outfits (user_id, occasion, generated_on);
=== wear_logs ===
-- Plan 06 (Stylist generator): outfits / outfit_items / wear_logs + flat RLS.
-- outfits also persist the chosen look_name + per-look garment layout so a saved
-- outfit re-renders identically (README §8).

create table public.outfits (
  id               uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id          uuid not null references public.profiles(id) on delete cascade,
  name             text,

);

create table public.wear_logs (
  id         uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),

# Executing Plans

## Overview

Load plan, review critically, execute all tasks, report when complete.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the executing-plans skill to implement this plan."

**Note:** Tell your human partner that Superpowers works much better with access to subagents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex App, Copilot CLI, and Gemini CLI all qualify; see the per-platform tool refs in `../using-superpowers/references/`). If subagents are available, use superpowers:subagent-driven-development instead of this skill.

## The Process

### Step 1: Load and Review Plan
1. Ensure an isolated workspace: use superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one
2. Read plan file
3. Review critically - identify any questions or concerns about the plan
4. If concerns: Raise them with your human partner before starting
5. If no concerns: Create todos for the plan items and proceed

### Step 2: Execute Tasks

For each task:
1. Mark as in_progress
2. Follow each step exactly (plan has bite-sized steps)
3. Run verifications as specified
4. Mark as completed

### Step 3: Complete Development

input.content:
-- One wear per outfit per day. The "Wear this today" button is a TOGGLE, and a
-- double tap (or a retried Server Action) must not produce two rows — every
-- wear count in the product is a count of these.
create unique index if not exists wear_logs_unique_day
  on public.wear_logs (user_id, outfit_id, worn_on)
  where outfit_id is not null;

-- Reading a wear back needs the outfit; reading the diary needs the date.
create index if not exists wear_logs_user_day_idx
  on public.wear_logs (user_id, worn_on desc);

-- The FK was declared with no ON DELETE action (NO ACTION), so deleting an
-- outfit that had been worn raised a foreign-key violation. saveDailyLooks is
-- delete-then-insert, so a Regenerate after a wear would have failed outright.
--
-- The primary fix lives in lib/outfits/daily.ts: a worn outfit is PINNED — it is
-- excluded from the day's delete, so it survives a Regenerate and stays in the
-- day's set. This constraint is the second line of defence, so any future delete
-- path degrades to "wear kept, outfit forgotten" instead of a 500.
alter table public.wear_logs
  drop constraint if exists wear_logs_outfit_id_fkey;
alter table public.wear_logs
  add constraint wear_logs_outfit_id_fkey
  foreign key (outfit_id) references public.outfits(id) on delete set null;

gh pr create --title "feat: outfit detail and wear logging" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Builds the outfit detail screen and the "Wear this today" action — the only
wear-log write path in the product. Times worn, cost-per-wear, last worn, the
Fit Diary grid, streaks, most-worn and gathering-dust are all views over what
this button writes, and nothing wrote to `wear_logs` before now.

## The latent bug this makes reachable, and fixes

`wear_logs.outfit_id` had no `ON DELETE` action, and `saveDailyLooks` is
delete-then-insert — so wearing a look and then regenerating the same day raised
a foreign-key violation and the regeneration failed outright.

A worn outfit is now **pinned**: `saveDailyLooks` excludes anything with a wear
log from the day's delete, and numbers the fresh set past it. The FK also
degrades to `ON DELETE SET NULL` as a second line of defence.

The plan's original fix was to null `generated_on` so the worn outfit left the
daily drop. That works, but the user-visible consequence is that tapping "Wear
this today" makes the look vanish from the stylist screen with no explanation.
Pinning keeps it visible and badged, and un-wearing just clears the badge.

A pinned look still **counts toward the day's three** — the re-ranker is asked
for `3 − pinned` fresh looks rather than a full set, so the day's set never grows
a fourth. The index tabs are 01/02/03 and a fourth does not fit at 390px.

A unique index on `(user_id, outfit_id, worn_on)` makes the toggle idempotent, so
a double tap or a retried action cannot inflate a wear count.

Also threads the outfit id through `loadDailyLooks`, which never selected it — so
until now a look on the stylist screen had nowhere to go.

## Stylist screen

- **"See the full look"** is the way into a look. Wrapping the flat-lay in an
  unlabelled link was tried first and is not discoverable — the flat-lay reads as
  a picture, not a control.
- **The credit line is gone.** The detail screen now lists every piece with its
  brand, image and category, and each row opens the same garment page — so the
  line was a second copy of that list costing ~200px of the fold.
- **Regenerate** was a bare uppercase line that read as a caption; an icon-only
  button beside the primary was tried and rejected (nothing tells you a ⟳ means
  "spend an AI call"). It is now a bounded secondary control with its words.
- The rust `f` glyph sat ~3px low: `align-middle` centres on x-height, and it
  carried a further downward nudge on top.

## Verified

Full suite green (324), tsc clean, build clean. Live on an iPhone 17 Pro
simulator and in the browser against the local stack: wear, unwear, double-tap
(exactly one row in the database, no duplicates), and a Regenerate after a wear —
the case that used to fail — which succeeded and produced a three-look set with
the worn look pinned at index 0.
EOF

**Design decisions made live with the user on this branch (all theirs):**

**`.screen-top` (app/globals.css) is now the single source for where a screen's content starts** —
`calc(env(safe-area-inset-top) + 22px)`. It replaced a hard-coded status-bar allowance on every screen

and inset only their overlay controls. ⚠️ Tailwind v4: never put a `pt-*` utility on the same element,
utilities beat components and would silently win.

`#201f22 → #0E0E10` is ~18 RGB levels, verbatim from the design handoff. It reads on the item detail
and capture confirm, where the stage is a bordered card; full-bleed against the canvas it does not.

**[PR #21](https://github.com/1curafu/Fitcheck/pull/21) is green** — yours to merge. Also did the housekeeping from #20 (branch deleted, plan moved to `done/`, queue #5 marked next).

**The safe-area fix.** One `.screen-top` utility in `globals.css` now carries `env(safe-area-inset-top)`, replacing the hard-coded status-bar allowance every screen had invented for itself. Measured before/after: **46px + the status bar → 28px** to first content, and **26px → 12px** under the nav pill. The bottom insets were the same mistake as `max(26px, …)` — floored instead of additive, so they never collapsed to zero in a browser where the toolbar already occupies that band.

**Three bugs turned up while verifying, all real:**

- **Back was dead on the outfit detail** when you land there directly — a shared link, a refresh, or a PWA cold start. `router.back()` with no history silently does nothing. - **The stylist screen lost your place** — you were right, and it was worse than just the look: a manual switch to Weekend also reverted to the predicted occasion. Both now live in the URL. Two traps in getting there: `useSearchParams()` doesn't observe `history.replaceState`, so my first attempt silently no-opped; and the geolocation refresh re-runs `generate`, so a consume-once restore got wiped by the second result.
- The detail stage had a hand-rolled copy of the `.surface-stage` gradient — now the design-system class.

On the gradient: it *is* rendering, it's just ~18 RGB levels by design. You chose to keep the handoff's values, so `.surface-stage` is unchanged — noted in `STATE.md` so it doesn't get re-litigated.

One caveat worth stating: the landing page and onboarding quiz got the same `.screen-top` change but I couldn't screenshot them — both are behind auth state you've already passed. The change is mechanical and the build is clean, but they're unverified visually.

What would you like to clarify?

For context, the decision is about one button on the item detail screen — "Style an outfit with this". The tension: Decision 5 says looks are generated **once per day** and tapping never calls the model, but styling around a piece you just picked is inherently on-demand. So the question is what that tap actually does, and what it costs you per user.

Happy to explain any part in more detail — the cost implications, how the quota seam would gate it, or what each option feels like to use.

content.text:
Measured on your actual closet: **62%** of items appear in today's looks — but that's with all 12 looks stored (every occasion generated). On a normal day where you open one or two occasions, it's roughly a quarter.

So the plan's "cheap path" mostly doesn't fire. Three taps in four fall through to generating anyway — it's the generation path wearing a disguise. And there's a second problem: a look that *happens to contain* your camel overshirt isn't a look *built around* it. You asked "style this"; showing you today's Work look because it includes those trousers answers a different question.

**Here's what I think is actually right, and it's a fourth option:**

Decision 5 isn't "never call the model" — it's *"never pay twice for the same question."* That's why the daily drop caches. A look built around a specific piece is a **new** question, so answering it is not a violation of Decision 5; answering it *repeatedly* would be.

So: pin the item → run the existing deterministic pipeline (`buildCandidates → rank → diversify` is pure TypeScript, free) → spend **one** Haiku call for the name and the "why" → **persist it like the daily drop**, keyed by item + day. Tap the same piece again and it's free. Gate the first call through `assertCanGenerate`, which is already the seam #7 will widen.

Why this is the better long-term shape:

- **The button always works** — any item, any day, no dead state and no "sorry, not in today's set".
- **Cost is bounded**, not per-tap: worst case one call per item per day, and the text-only re-rank is well under a cent. Caching makes repeat taps free.
- **It reuses everything** — same pipeline, same `outfits` table, same quota seam. No new architecture.
- **It's a better paywall than hiding the button.** README has this as Pro-only; I'd rather free users get a few stylings a day and *feel* the ceiling. A feature you've used and want more of converts; a feature you've never seen doesn't.

The cost versus the plan's version is smaller than it looks, because the plan already generates on ~75% of taps — it just doesn't cache the result.

input.new_string:
## ⚠️ DECIDED 2026-07-30 — the cheap reading below was REJECTED. Task 5 is rewritten.

**Resolution: pin the item, generate once, PERSIST and cache it.** Tapping pins the item into candidate
building, runs the deterministic pipeline, spends **one** Haiku call for the name and the why, and
stores the result keyed by `(user, item, local date)`. Tapping the same piece again that day is a free
read. Gated by `assertCanGenerate`, so queue #7 widens it without touching this screen.

Two things settled it:

1. **The cheap reading is not cheap.** Measured on the real 21-item closet with all 12 of today's looks
   stored (a heavy day — every occasion opened): only **62%** of the closet appears in today's looks. On
   an ordinary day with one or two occasions generated it is roughly a quarter. So ~3 taps in 4 fell
   through to the generation branch *anyway*, and that branch did not cache — costing MORE over a day
   than generating once per item and storing it.
2. **It answered the wrong question.** A look that happens to *contain* the piece is not a look built
   *around* it. "Style this" asked for the second.

**Decision 5 is not violated.** Decision 5 says never pay twice for a question already answered — which
is why the daily drop caches. A look built around a specific piece is a NEW question; answering it once
and persisting it is that principle applied on a second axis, not an exception to it.

Also rejected: an AI call on every tap (unbounded, and the largest per-user cost in the product), and
filter-only with no generation (the CTA is dead for most of the closet on most days).

**Tier note:** `README.md:33` marks this CTA **Pro**. This design makes that unnecessary as a hard gate —
it consumes the same generation meter, so free users get a few stylings a day and feel the ceiling. A
feature you have used and want more of converts; one you have never seen does not. Queue #7 decides the
number; nothing here needs to change for it.

content.text: Found a real bug — SQL says this item has 1 wear, the screen says 0. `wear_logs` and `outfit_items` aren't directly related (both hang off `outfits`), so PostgREST can't embed them:

input.old_string:
/**
   * Wear history for ONE item.
   *
   * A wear is logged against an OUTFIT, never an item, so an item's wear count
   * is "how many logged outfits contained it": wear_logs → outfit_items. The
   * `!inner` is what makes the embed a restriction rather than a nullable join —
   * without it every wear log in the account comes back and every item claims
   * the same wear count.
   */
  const { data: logs } = await supabase
    .from("wear_logs")
    .select("worn_on, outfit_items!inner(item_id)")
    .eq("outfit_items.item_id", itemId);
input.new_string:
/**
   * Wear history for ONE item, in two steps on purpose.
   *
   * A wear is logged against an OUTFIT, never an item, so an item's wear count
   * is "how many logged outfits contained it". `wear_logs` and `outfit_items`
   * are NOT directly related — both hang off `outfits` — so PostgREST cannot
   * embed one in the other, and an `outfit_items!inner(...)` join silently
   * returned zero rows for an item that had genuinely been worn. Two explicit
   * queries are obviously correct where that embed was quietly wrong.
   */
  const { data: wornIn } = await supabase
    .from("outfit_items")
    .select("outfit_id")
    .eq("item_id", itemId);
  const outfitIds = (wornIn ?? []).map((r) => r.outfit_id);
  const { data: logs } = outfitIds.length
    ? await supabase.from("wear_logs").select("worn_on").in("outfit_id", outfitIds)
    : { data: [] };

Queue #5 (`item-detail-rebuild`). Item detail was a tag form; the design calls it
the canonical screen, and it answers "how do I actually wear this?" — cutout as
hero, wear stats, formality, tags, what it goes with. Editing moved behind `⋯`.

## The decision this plan was blocked on

"Style an outfit with this" conflicted with Decision 5 (looks are a daily drop;
tapping never calls the model). The plan assumed the cheap reading — filter
today's stored looks, fall back to an uncached generation. **Measured and
rejected:** on the real 21-item closet with all 12 of today's looks stored, only
**62%** of the closet appears in them; on an ordinary day with one or two
occasions generated it is roughly a quarter. So ~3 taps in 4 fell through to
generating anyway, and threw the result away — costing more over a day, not
less. It also answered the wrong question: a look that *contains* a piece is not
a look built *around* it.

**Implemented instead: pin, generate once, cache.** The piece is pinned, the
deterministic pipeline runs, ONE text call names and explains the result, and it
is persisted keyed by `(user, item, local day)`. Second tap that day is a free
read — measured 9.7s → 256ms. Gated by `assertCanGenerate`, so queue #7 widens it
without touching this screen.

This does not bypass Decision 5. That decision says never pay twice for a
question already answered; "what goes with this piece?" is a new question, so it
gets its answer cached the same way the daily drop does.

Pinning happens by dropping same-category rivals **before** candidate building,
not by filtering after — filtering after would have to survive the 200-combo
CAP, and a piece that missed the cut would silently produce "no looks", the same
class of bug as the coverage defect in #14.

## Keeping styled looks out of the daily drop

`outfits.styled_item_id` + a partial unique index is the cache key. `look_index`
stays NULL so `outfits_daily_unique` cannot collide (Postgres treats NULLs as
distinct). `loadDailyLooks` and `saveDailyLooks` both filter `styled_item_id is
null` — without that the styled look renders as a fourth look and the next
regenerate deletes the cache. Verified: 3 looks in the drop, styled row
untouched by a regeneration.

## Bugs found while verifying

- **Wear counts read 0 for items that had been worn.** `wear_logs` and
  `outfit_items` are not directly related — both hang off `outfits` — so the
  `outfit_items!inner(...)` embed silently returned nothing. Two explicit
  queries now. Caught by checking the screen against SQL rather than trusting it.
- **A React key warning**: `page.tsx` is a Server Component and passed the
  `StyleCta` element across the RSC boundary as a prop; a serialised element has
  no positional identity, so React demanded a key. `ItemDetail` is already a
  client component and has `item.id`, so it builds the CTA itself.

## Also

- **Prices are EUR**, not the plan's GBP (`en-IE` → "€50.00" for the English UI).
- Tile values share one size with bottom-aligned labels — different sizes left
  the third label off the line the other two shared.
- The subtitle no longer repeats a name identical to the subcategory.

## Verified

360 tests, tsc clean, build clean. Live against the local stack and on an
iPhone 17 Pro simulator: wear count checked against SQL, an unpriced item hides
the cost tile entirely, goes-with links open their garment, both CTA paths, and
the styled look staying out of the daily drop across a regeneration.

Local dev data: a price was set on one item to exercise the cost-per-wear tile.

so about cheap reading, is it generate new outfit sets or not so good as it can be?

Good question — and the honest answer is: **yes, it generates a genuinely new outfit**, but there are three real quality gaps worth naming.

**What it actually does.** It doesn't filter today's looks. It rebuilds from your whole closet with the piece pinned, scores every valid combination, and asks the model to pick the best one. So the result is a real styling, not a lookup — that part is as good as the daily drop.

**Where it's weaker than the daily drop, and one of these is my doing:**

1. **I skipped `diversify`.** The daily generate does `diversify(ranked, 20)` before the model sees anything, precisely because ranking *clusters* — a neutral top harmonises with everything, so the raw top 20 are near-identical. I used `pinned.slice(0, 20)`. The model still picks a good outfit, but it's choosing between 20 variations of one idea rather than 20 genuinely different ones, so you get the safest combination rather than the most interesting. That's a one-line fix using machinery that already exists, and I think it's worth doing.

2. **It returns one look, not three.** I chose `want: 1` to keep cost down. Styling around a piece is arguably where you'd *most* want options — "here are two ways to wear this."

3. **It's cached all day with no way to ask for another.** This is the one I'd worry about most as a user experience: tap it a second time and you get the identical look with no explanation. On the stylist screen that same situation has a visible Regenerate; here it just looks like the button stopped working.

Note that 2 and 3 compound — one look, and no way to get a different one until tomorrow.

**What I'd do:** add `diversify` (strictly better, no cost change), and give the screen a quiet "try another" that spends one call through the same quota seam — the exact pattern Regenerate already uses. That keeps the cache as the default free path while making the feature feel alive instead of frozen.

### Suspects, in order of prior probability

**S1 — the pipeline is deterministic, so Regenerate legitimately returns the same looks.**

# Styled Look Depth Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Make "Style an outfit with this" as good as the daily drop. It currently returns one safe
look and then freezes for the rest of the day.

**Architecture:** No new machinery. Task 1 reuses `diversify`, which the daily path already calls and
the styled path does not. Tasks 2–4 widen the styled look from one to a small set and add an explicit
"try another", metered through the ledger that queue #8 builds.

**Tech Stack:** Next.js 16 App Router, Supabase, Vitest.

## Why this exists

Written 2026-07-31, after PR #22 shipped the feature and the user asked whether the styled look is
"generating a new outfit set or not so good as it can be". It generates a genuinely new outfit — it
rebuilds from the whole closet with the piece pinned, it does not filter today's looks — but three
things hold it below the daily drop. All three were confirmed against the merged code, not assumed.

## ⚠️ Read before writing anything — what is ALREADY decided elsewhere

This plan was written *after* checking the rest of the queue, specifically so it does not re-decide
things other plans own. Do not relitigate these:

| Question | Already answered by | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| Is styling free or paid? | `MONETISATION.md:87` | On the **meter**; unlimited on Pro. Pro feature #2. |
| Where does the meter live? | `todo/2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` (queue #8) | `generation_events`, an append-only ledger. `assertCanGenerate` is the seam and `style-actions.ts` already calls it. |
| Is "limited" an error? | queue #8 | **No — a first-class status.** `StyleCta` already renders a `limited` state; PR #22 built it that way deliberately. |
| Should Decision 5 forbid this? | `done/2026-07-24-item-detail-rebuild.md` | No. Decision 5 forbids paying twice for the *same* question; styling a chosen piece is a different question, so it gets its own cached answer. |

**Sequencing:** Task 1 is independent and can ship on its own at any time. **Tasks 2–4 must come after
queue #8**, because they spend the meter that plan defines. Executing them earlier means inventing a
second counting scheme, which is exactly what queue #8 exists to prevent.

**A defect in queue #8 that this plan depends on:** `generation_events.is_regenerate` is a boolean, and
a styled generation is neither the day's free drop for an occasion (`false` would mark that occasion as
already dropped) nor a regenerate of one (`true` would make styling eat the regenerate allowance). A
note has been added to that plan's schema to replace the boolean with `kind text` —
`'drop' | 'regenerate' | 'styled'`. **If it is still a boolean when you get here, fix it there, not
here.**

## Source

`design_handoff_stylist_generator/Fitcheck.dc.html:587-657` (item detail). Feature as shipped:
`app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts`, `components/closet/style-cta.tsx`, `lib/outfits/styled.ts`,
`lib/outfits/styled-store.ts`.

## File structure

| File | Responsibility | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts` | Diversify the shortlist; return a set; honour "try another" | Modify |
| `lib/outfits/styled-store.ts` | Load/save a SET of styled looks | Modify |
| `lib/outfits/styled.ts` | Pure helpers | Modify |
| `components/closet/style-cta.tsx` | Index tabs + "try another" | Modify |
| `supabase/migrations/*_styled_look_index.sql` | Allow >1 styled look per item per day | **Create** (Task 2) |

---

### Task 1: Diversify the styled shortlist — independent, ship any time

**Files:** Modify `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts`; append to `lib/outfits/__tests__/styled.test.ts`

The daily path does `diversify(ranked, 20)` before the model sees anything; the styled path does
`pinned.slice(0, 20)`. Ranking **clusters** — a neutral top harmonises with everything, so the raw top
20 are near-identical and the model is choosing between 20 variations of one idea. This is the same
reasoning that produced `lib/generator/diversity.ts` in PR #14/#15; it was simply never applied to the
second consumer.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test.** Prove the shortlist the model receives is not 20 versions of
one outfit. Build a ranked list where the top entries share a bottom, assert
`shortlistFor(pinned)` yields more distinct bottoms than `pinned.slice(0, 20)` does. Put
`shortlistFor` in `lib/outfits/styled.ts` so it is testable without the action.

- [ ] **Step 2: Run it — expect FAIL**

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement.** `shortlistFor(pinned, n = 20)` = `diversify(pinned, n)`. Replace
`pinned.slice(0, 20)` in the action with it.
  - ⚠️ `diversify` backfills to a floor so a small closet still returns something — confirm the pinned
    piece is still present in every returned combo, since `diversify` is only reordering a list that
    `pinItem` already filtered.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run it — expect PASS**

- [ ] **Step 5: Verify live.** Style the same piece on two different days (or clear the cached row) and
confirm the look is not simply the highest-scoring combination every time.

- [ ] **Step 6: Commit** — `git commit -m "fix(closet): the styled shortlist is diversified like the daily one"`

---

### Task 2: A styled SET, not a single look

**Files:** migration; modify `lib/outfits/styled-store.ts`, `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts`

`want: 1` was chosen to bound cost. Styling around a piece is arguably where options matter most —

**Decision to make before coding, and state it in the PR:** how many? The daily drop is three and the
index tabs are built for `01/02/03`. **Recommendation: two.** One AI call returns both (the re-ranker
already takes `want`), the cost is unchanged, and two is enough to feel like a choice without implying
this screen is a second daily drop.

- [ ] **Step 1: The migration.** `outfits_styled_unique` is currently
`(user_id, styled_item_id, generated_on)` — one row per piece per day, which now blocks a set. Replace
it with `(user_id, styled_item_id, generated_on, look_index)`.

The cache is right, and the missing affordance is what makes it feel wrong: tap a second time and the
identical look returns with no explanation. The stylist screen solved exactly this with a visible,
worded Regenerate — and PR #20 established that an icon alone is not enough, because nothing tells you
a `⟳` means "spend an AI call".

- [ ] **Step 1:** Add a `regenerate?: boolean` argument to `styleWithItem`. When true, skip the cache
read, record the generation as `kind: 'styled'`, and REPLACE the stored set (delete-then-insert, the
same reasoning as `saveDailyLooks`: a new run may return a different number of looks and leftovers must
not survive beside them).

- [ ] **Step 2:** ⚠️ **Exclude the pieces the user just saw**, or "try another" returns the same look

penalty (`RECENT_WEIGHT`) — use it. **Do NOT use `excludeItemIds`**: a hard exclusion was measured and
rejected on this closet (0 combos in winter), and here it is worse, because the pinned piece must never
be excluded from a look built around it.

PR #20 arrived at after an icon-only version was tried and rejected.

Done. `main` is at `f3eafa3`, branch cleaned, plan moved to `done/`.

**On whether the three points are really valuable — my honest read after checking the queue:**

Point 1 (**diversify**) is the one I'd call a defect rather than an enhancement. The daily path diversifies its shortlist precisely because ranking clusters; the styled path doesn't, so the model picks between 20 variations of one idea. It's a one-line fix reusing existing machinery, and I marked it **independent — shippable any time**, not blocked behind the meter.

Points 2 and 3 (**more than one look**, **try another**) are real but genuinely blocked on queue #8, since they spend the meter that plan defines.

**Checking the other plans stopped me making two redundant decisions, and turned up one defect:**

- **`MONETISATION.md:87` had already decided the tier question** — styling is on the meter, unlimited on Pro. So "try another" needed no new policy, just the affordance. I'd have re-litigated that.
- **Queue #8 already owns the counting** (`generation_events`, `limited`-as-a-status). My plan defers to it rather than inventing a second scheme — and `StyleCta` already renders that `limited` state, so PR #22 is compatible.
- **A real defect in queue #8:** `generation_events.is_regenerate` is a *boolean*, and a styled generation is neither the day's free drop for an occasion (recording `false` would mark that occasion as already dropped) nor a regenerate of one (`true` would make styling eat the regenerate allowance). I wrote the fix into that plan's schema — replace the boolean with `kind text` — so it's caught by whoever executes #8, not discovered afterwards.

I also flagged a trap in Task 2: styled rows keep `look_index` NULL *deliberately*, so giving them a real index to store a set would reintroduce a collision with the daily-drop unique index.

Written up in:
- **`docs/STATE.md`** — PR #22 summary plus the two gotchas worth remembering beyond this feature (the `wear_logs`/`outfit_items` embed returning zero rows silently, and JSX crossing the RSC boundary earning a key warning), and the local price edit I made.
- **`todo/2026-07-31-styled-look-depth.md`** — the new plan, with an up-front table of what's already decided elsewhere so it doesn't get re-argued.
- **README** — queue #11, and the "Style an outfit with this" open decision marked closed with the reasoning.

Queue #6, `fit-diary`, is next.
